subject: 1512FD2C8B8042FA84CBA88AE4FD2A7C
introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s opening sentence is blunt: “As soon as they begin to differ, both are wrong.” The readings then build what is meant to prevent it: one appointed interpreter, an elected body for what the text leaves open, signed and sealed writings as the only authority, reported talks and pilgrims’ notes as hearsay, and, at the end, freedom for every believer to study and to voice a view that binds no one. Many of the outside voices know the same problems. An official on the road to Gaza cannot understand without a guide, Paul signs his letters against forgeries, Ben Sira’s grandson apologizes for his translation, and Socrates explains why a written text cannot answer for itself. Others push back. Mill holds that one who knows only his own side knows little of that, Locke makes reason the last judge, Emerson lets each reader interpret by the spirit, and the rabbis, whom one reading calls fossilized, describe a single verse breaking into many meanings under the hammer.
questions: “As soon as two parties begin to differ, both are wrong.” Saxe’s blind men are each partly right and all wrong; Mill thinks hearing the other side is how one learns one’s own. What kind of differing do the readings condemn, and what kind do the last readings protect?

Socrates says a written text keeps a solemn silence when questioned; one reading blames “Sufficient unto us is the Book” for centuries of conflict. What can a living interpreter do for a text, and what are the risks?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá accepts only what bears his hand or seal, and Paul gives his signature as “the token in every epistle.” Yet Luke’s Gospel and Thucydides’s speeches are reports. How should a reader treat a moving saying whose source cannot be checked?

Personal interpretations “can be most illuminating” but may never become a standard or a cause of dispute. Set this beside Milton’s “opinion in good men is but knowledge in the making.” How could a study group practise both?

One reading contrasts these interpretations with those “of the Rabbis and the Church.” Having read the saying of the hammer and the stone and the scribe’s treasure of things new and old, how would you state the contrast fairly?

outside.why: “As soon as they begin to differ, both are wrong.” Saxe’s blind men, disputing over the elephant, come to nearly the same verdict: each was partly in the right, and all were in the wrong.

The reading treats a difference between two parties as the fault of both. Mill thinks a person who has never heard the other side hardly knows his own: he who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that. Can difference be a way of learning before it is a wrong?
What is not understood is to be asked of “Him Who is their Source.” The official on the road to Gaza, asked if he understands what he reads, answers: how can I, except some man should guide me?
“Beware lest ye find differences therein.” The Qur’án describes its own verses as clear and allegorical, and says that those with doubt in their hearts pursue the allegorical, seeking dissension.

Bahá’u’lláh “has shut the door to such differences.” Paul begs a divided congregation for the same thing: that there be no divisions among you, but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind.
Human reason “cannot surround the Reality Itself.” Paul on the limits of every interpreter, himself included: we know in part, and we prophesy in part.

Reason is called faulty, and so unfit to settle the meaning of the Word. Locke replies that there is nothing else to settle it with: reason must be our last judge and guide in every thing. With what faculty does a reader recognize an authorized interpreter?

Twelve centuries of traditions about the Promised One, and “not a single word thereof was adorned with … truth.” Jesus’s charge against the learned of his day: ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition.
A Book is not enough without an interpreter. Socrates says why a written text cannot defend itself: ask it a question and it preserves a solemn silence, and it always needs its parent to protect it.

“Sufficient unto us is the Book of God” is named as the root of division. The Second Letter to Timothy speaks of scripture in terms close to sufficiency: profitable for doctrine and correction, that the man of God may be throughly furnished. Is the danger in the claim, or in who makes it?

“Be your own interpreter” is given as the slogan of those who would be free of the Covenant. Emerson states the same idea as a principle: every scripture is to be interpreted by the same spirit which gave it forth. What separates his reader from theirs?
Some would “make whatever we conceive in our imagination the foundation of the Faith.” The Second Letter of Peter: no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.

“If a soul … utters an explanation which does not harm the Cause, do not oppose him.” Jesus says the same when the disciples want to stop a man outside their company: forbid him not, for he that is not against us is on our part.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá is the interpreter of the “aims, intents, and purposes” of his Father’s words. On the road to Emmaus the risen Jesus does this for the scriptures: beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded the things concerning himself.

“Anyone quoting me must have authority written either with my own hand, or tablets signed with my seal.” Paul marks his letters the same way: the salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle.
Statements had been attributed to ‘Abdu’l-Bahá “of which I am innocent.” Paul had the same trouble and warns his readers not to be shaken by letter as from us.

Deduction belongs to an elected body, and the conclusions of individual scholars have no authority without it. In the Talmud’s best-known story one sage has miracles on his side and the majority decides against him: it is not in heaven.

“The early translations are far from being accurate, no matter who the translator may be.” The grandson of Ben Sira, about 130 BCE, asks pardon for his own: things uttered in Hebrew and translated into another tongue have not the same force in them.

“No authority can be attached to a mere hearsay, no matter through whom it may come.” Paine uses the same word against all reported revelation. The readings apply it to reports and keep the signed text; he applies it to everything after the first hearer.

Talks taken down by others cannot claim the authority of a revealed Tablet. Thucydides admits what such records are: it was difficult to carry the speeches word for word in memory, so he gives what the occasion demanded, keeping to the general sense. What is a reader owed about how a speech reached the page?

A pilgrim’s note has no authority even when the writer is reliable and several agree. Luke introduces his Gospel as an orderly account of what eyewitnesses delivered. How does a tradition decide which reports become scripture?

The notes are not authoritative, yet they carry “information and suggestions of a most precious character.” John ends by admitting how much was never written: the world itself could not contain the books.
Believers are invited to immerse themselves in the ocean of the words. Ben Bag Bag on the Torah: turn it over, and again turn it over, for all is therein; grow gray and old in it.
Authoritative interpretation does not stop anyone’s own study. The people of Berea are praised for searching the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

A personal view is welcome but “can never be upheld as a standard,” and disputes are not to arise from it. Milton expects much arguing wherever there is much desire to learn, and asks only for a little forbearance. Can views be voiced freely where dispute is ruled out?

The reading sets these interpretations against those “of the Rabbis and the Church,” which it calls a fossilization. The rabbis described their own practice otherwise: as a hammer breaks a stone into many fragments, one verse yields several explanations.

Interpretation that illuminates and does not supplant. Jesus’s picture of the trained scribe is of a householder who bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old. Would the rabbis and the Church recognize themselves in the reading’s account of them?

thucydides-speeches-word-for-word.text: With reference to the speeches in this history, some were delivered before the war began, others while it was going on; some I heard myself, others I got from various quarters; it was in all cases difficult to carry them word for word in one's memory, so my habit has been to make the speakers say what was in my opinion demanded of them by the various occasions, of course adhering as closely as possible to the general sense of what they really said
thucydides-speeches-word-for-word.author: Thucydides

sirach-not-the-same-force.text: For the same things uttered in Hebrew, and translated into another tongue, have not the same force in them: and not only these things, but the law itself, and the prophets, and the rest of the books, have no small difference, when they are spoken in their own language
